We use the convention that indices are taken modulo $2$ , so that $j+1=1$ when $j=2$ . Here, the Kepler potential comes from the leading long-range interaction between the two copies of $Q$ . This approximation remains valid for $m$ -solitons with arbitrary $m\geq 2$ as was recently generalized in [19]; the effective dynamics of $m$ -solitons is governed by the $m$ -body problem.

In (1.9), the center of mass evolves freely: $\lambda_{1}\ddot{\alpha}_{2}+\lambda_{2}\ddot{\alpha}_{1}=0$ . We will normalize the center of mass by assuming

$$ \lambda_{1}\alpha_{2}+\lambda_{2}\alpha_{1}=0 $$

throughout the paper. The two-body problem also admits the conserved energy

$$ E_{0}:=|\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}|^{2}-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}}\right)\frac{1}{|\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1}|}. $$

It follows that if the two bodies do not collide initially, that is, $\alpha_{1}(0)\neq\alpha_{2}(0)$ , then they remain away from each other for all time. Let $\alpha=\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1}$ . Then global solutions to (1.9) can be classified according to the sign of $E_{0}$ or, equivalently, the growth rate of $|\alpha(t)|$ :

- • Hyperbolic: if $E_{0}>0$ , then $|\alpha(t)|\sim t$ as $t\to\infty$ and $\alpha(t)$ describes a hyperbola.

- • Parabolic: if $E_{0}=0$ , then $|\alpha(t)|\sim t^{\frac{2}{3}}$ as $t\to\infty$ and $\alpha(t)$ describes a parabola.

- • Elliptic: if $E_{0}<0$ , then $|\alpha(t)|$ is bounded and $\alpha(t)$ describes an ellipse.

In both the hyperbolic case and the parabolic case, we have $|\alpha(t)|\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$ , so we say these are expansive cases. For expansive dynamics, the separation between the two solitons tends to infinity, weakening the soliton interaction over time. Therefore, one may hope to construct solutions to the Hartree equation (1.1) that, as time goes to infinity, approach two-solitons or multisolitons whose center dynamics is described by an expansive solution to the two-body problem or the $m$ -body problem. In particular, [9] constructed two-soliton solutions to the Hartree equation whose center dynamics approaches an expansive solution to (1.9), while [19] constructed multisoliton solutions whose trajectories approach some classes of expansive solutions to the $m$ -body problem. The recent parallel results for the four-dimensional Hartree equation in [6, 17] also considered expansive solutions to the adapted $m$ -body problem. In general, expansive dynamics is more approachable because of the decay of the interaction error in time, and known results on multisoliton solutions of Hartree equations have mainly focused on expansive trajectories.

By contrast, in the elliptic case, the solitons remain at bounded separation, so the long-range interaction between the solitons persists. One cannot expect the small interaction errors to decay by waiting for large times. This makes the elliptic trajectory much more delicate to study. Until now, there has been no construction of solutions to the Hartree equation (1.1) whose asymptotic behavior is governed by elliptic solutions to (1.9).

The main result:

In this paper, we consider two-soliton solutions to (1.1) with elliptic trajectories. To the author’s knowledge, this is the first work to study elliptic center dynamics for the Hartree equation. Even in strongly interacting multisoliton regimes for other models such as [15, 8], there is usually still some decay of the interaction error in time. Therefore, the elliptic regime considered in this paper represents a genuinely new dynamical setting.

Our result proves the finite-time stability of two-soliton solutions with approximate elliptic trajectories. As has been explained, the interaction remains of fixed size along the elliptic orbit, so the smallness of the error must come from the order of the approximation rather than from time decay. We thus do not study asymptotic behavior as time tends to infinity; instead, we prove finite-time stability for carefully chosen profiles.

#### Theorem 1.

Given $\delta>0$ , $C_{e}>0$ and $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0$ , there exist $\nu>0$ , $\bar{r}_{0}>0$ such that for any $r_{0}>\bar{r}_{0}$ , there exists $\kappa>0$ with the following property.

If $(\alpha_{1}(t),\alpha_{2}(t),\beta_{1}(t),\beta_{2}(t),\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})$ is an elliptic solution to (1.9) with

$$ r_{0}\leq|\alpha_{2}(t)-\alpha_{1}(t)|\leq C_{e}r_{0},\quad\forall t\geq 0 $$

and $\gamma_{1}(t)$ , $\gamma_{2}(t)$ satisfy

$$ \dot{\gamma}_{j}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}-|\beta_{j}|^{2}-\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot\alpha_{j}+\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1}|},\quad j=1,2, $$

then there exists $R_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ with

$$ \left\|R_{0}-\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}Q\Big(\frac{\cdot-\alpha_{j}(0)}{\lambda_{j}}\Big)e^{i\gamma_{j}(0)+i\beta_{j}(0)\cdot x}\right\|_{H^{1}}\lesssim_{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}}r_{0}^{-3} $$

such that for $u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ , $\|u_{0}-R_{0}\|_{H^{1}}<\kappa$ implies

$$ \left\|u(t)-\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}Q\Big(\frac{\cdot-\alpha_{j}(t)}{\lambda_{j}}\Big)e^{i\gamma_{j}(t)+i\beta_{j}(t)\cdot x}\right\|_{H^{1}}<\delta,\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq\nu r_{0}^{2}, $$

where $u$ is the solution to (1.1) with $u(0)=u_{0}$ .

#### Remark 1.1.

The period of the ellipse $\alpha_{2}(t)-\alpha_{1}(t)$ has size $r_{0}^{3/2}$ , so the time scale $r_{0}^{2}$ on which we establish stability is much longer than the period. In other words, the two-soliton solution will remain close to the elliptic orbit for many cycles before, if ever, departing from it.

#### Remark 1.2.

The $\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1}|}$ term in the equation for $\gamma_{j}$ is nonstandard. We call it an interaction shift and it is necessary in the construction of approximate solutions. See Remark 3.1 for further explanation.

#### Remark 1.3.

The assumption $r_{0}\leq|\alpha_{2}(t)-\alpha_{1}(t)|\leq C_{e}r_{0}$ means that the elliptic trajectory has size $r_{0}$ and uniformly bounded eccentricity. The eccentricity bound is necessary for establishing the stability of the center dynamics in Proposition 4.2.

#### Remark 1.4.

We will construct approximate profiles $V_{1},V_{2}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ close to $Q$ and take

$$ R_{0}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}V_{j}\Big(\frac{x-\alpha_{j}(0)}{\lambda_{j}}\Big)e^{i\gamma_{j}(0)+i\beta_{j}(0)\cdot x}. $$

Here $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ encode higher-order correction terms compensating for the long-range effect of the Hartree equation. This is why $R_{0}$ is only required to be within $O(r_{0}^{-3})$ in $H^{1}$ of the naive two-soliton profile in (1.14).

As shown in the proof of the theorem in Section 5, the profiles $V_{1},V_{2}$ depend on

$$ \alpha_{2}(0)-\alpha_{1}(0),\;\;\beta_{2}(0)-\beta_{1}(0),\;\;\lambda_{1},\;\;\lambda_{2},\;\;\gamma_{1}(0),\;\;\gamma_{2}(0). $$

Consequently, $R_{0}$ depends on the initial parameters

$$ \alpha_{1}(0),\;\;\alpha_{2}(0),\;\;\beta_{1}(0),\;\;\beta_{2}(0),\;\;\lambda_{1},\;\;\lambda_{2},\;\;\gamma_{1}(0),\;\;\gamma_{2}(0). $$

The proof follows the same broad modulation strategy as [9, 19], but the elliptic setting changes both the role of the approximate solution and the order to which it must be constructed. In the expansive cases considered there, the separation between solitons tends to infinity, so interaction errors tend to $0$ as time tends to $\infty$ . Therefore, when the order of approximation is high enough, the error decays nearly exponentially in time. In the elliptic case in this paper, the separation remains comparable to the fixed parameter $r_{0}$ along the elliptic orbit. Thus the main point is to construct an approximate solution whose error is small uniformly on the relevant time interval. By introducing a cutoff in (3.12) when defining approximate solutions and keeping track of the dependence of all constants on the approximation order $N$ , it turns out that $N$ should be chosen proportional to the separation $r_{0}$ (see Remark 3.10), although this relation is not apparent from the approximation scheme itself.

More precisely, the proof has three main ingredients. First, in Section 3, we construct an $N$ -th order approximate two-soliton and prove that its error is exponentially small in $r_{0}$ when $N\sim r_{0}$ . Second, in Section 4, we show that the approximate center dynamics remains close to the elliptic Kepler dynamics on the required time scale. Third, in Section 5, we use modulation and a localized coercive energy functional to control the difference between the true solution and the approximate profile. We also collect preparatory properties of the linearized operators in Section 2.

The construction scheme of approximate solutions and the localized energy estimate are closest to [9, 19]. The new difficulties arise from the bounded separation of elliptic trajectories. They are addressed by the lower-order cancellations in Proposition 3.4 using the interaction shift in Remark 3.1, the quantitative accuracy estimate in Proposition 3.9 using the cutoff in the dipole expansion (3.12), and the stability analysis of the approximate elliptic center dynamics in Proposition 4.2.

## 2. Linearized operators around the ground state

In this section, we study some properties of the linearized operators around the ground state. Write $u=e^{it}(Q+\varepsilon)$ . Using (1.6), we can rewrite (1.1) as

$$ \partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{Re}\ \varepsilon\\
\mathrm{Im}\ \varepsilon\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0&-L_{-}\\
L_{+}&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{Re}\ \varepsilon\\
\mathrm{Im}\ \varepsilon\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{Im}\ \mathcal{N}(Q,\varepsilon)\\
-\mathrm{Re}\ \mathcal{N}(Q,\varepsilon)\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $\mathcal{N}$ is of second or higher order in $\varepsilon$ , and $L_{+},L_{-}$ , the linearized operators around $Q$ , are defined by

$$ L_{+}f:=-\Delta f+f+\phi_{Q^{2}}f+2\phi_{Qf}Q,\quad L_{-}f:=-\Delta f+f+\phi_{Q^{2}}f. $$

The kernels of $L_{\pm}$ necessarily contain modes generated by the symmetries of (1.1). From [10], we know the ground state $Q$ is non-degenerate, meaning that the kernels of $L_{\pm}$ consist precisely of those symmetry directions:

$$ \ker(L_{+})=\text{span}\{\partial_{1}Q,\partial_{2}Q,\partial_{3}Q\},\quad\ker(L_{-})=\text{span}\{Q\}. $$

Let $\Lambda=2+x\cdot\nabla$ . We recall [19, Lemma 4.4].

#### Lemma 2.1.

There exist $\delta,c>0$ such that if $v\in H^{1}$ is real-valued, then

$$ \begin{gathered}|(v,Q)|+|(v,xQ)|<\delta\|v\|_{H^{1}}\implies(L_{+}v,v)\geq c\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2},\\
|(v,\Lambda Q)|<\delta\|v\|_{H^{1}}\implies(L_{-}v,v)\geq c\|v\|_{H^{1}}^{2}.\end{gathered} $$

The main purpose of this section is to prove the following quantitative version of Lemma 2.4 in [9]. In particular, it shows that when $L_{\pm}^{-1}$ is applied to an exponentially decaying function, the exponential decay rate does not weaken, and the weighted $L^{\infty}$ norm is uniform.

#### Lemma 2.2.

There exist universal constants $c,C>0$ such that the following holds. If $f$ is a real-valued function with $|f(x)|\leq e^{-c|x|}$ , then

- (1) $(f,\nabla Q)=0\implies\exists u$ such that $L_{+}u=f$ and $|u(x)|\leq Ce^{-c|x|}$ ;

- (2) $(f,Q)=0\implies\exists u$ such that $L_{-}u=f$ and $|u(x)|\leq Ce^{-c|x|}$ .

#### Proof.

[9, Lemma 2.4] asserts the existence of $u$ . It remains to show the estimate. Let $C_{0}>0$ and $c_{0}>0$ be such that $Q(x)\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}|x|}$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . These are universal constants. We claim that taking $c<\min\{c_{0},1\}$ suffices.

We first prove (1). Since $\nabla Q\in\ker(L_{+})$ , we have $L_{+}(u+a\cdot\nabla Q)=f$ for any $a\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . Note $(\nabla Q,xQ)$ is invertible. By choosing $a$ properly so that $(u+a\cdot\nabla Q,xQ)=0$ , we may replace $u$ by this representative and assume $(u,xQ)=0$ . Then by Lemma 2.1, one has

$$ (f,u)=(L_{+}u,u)\geq C^{-1}\|u\|_{H^{1}}^{2}-C(u,Q)^{2}. $$

Note that $(u,2Q)=-(u,L_{+}(\Lambda Q))=-(f,\Lambda Q)$ . We deduce

$$ \|u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\|u\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\leq C(f,u)+C(f,\Lambda Q)^{2}. $$

By Cauchy–Schwarz, we get the uniform bound

$$ \|u\|_{L^{2}}\leq C. $$

The equation for $u$ can be written as

$$ \displaystyle u \displaystyle=(-\Delta+1)^{-1}f-(-\Delta+1)^{-1}\big(\phi_{Q^{2}}u+2\phi_{Qu}Q\big). $$

In three dimensions, the kernel of $(-\Delta+1)^{-1}$ is $\frac{e^{-|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}$ . Then we have

$$ u(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}f(y)\mathrm{d}y-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}\big(\phi_{Q^{2}}(y)u(y)+2\phi_{Qu}(y)Q(y)\big)\mathrm{d}y. $$

Fix any $M>0$ . We want to estimate $\min\{M,e^{c|x|}\}|u(x)|$ . We first have

$$ e^{c|x|}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}f(y)\mathrm{d}y\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-(1-c)|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}\mathrm{d}y\leq C. $$

Take a universal constant $L>0$ such that

$$ \sup_{|y|\geq L}|\phi_{Q^{2}}(y)|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|x|}}{4\pi|x|}\mathrm{d}x<\frac{1}{2}. $$

Then using Hölder’s inequality and Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev’s inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle\ e^{c|x|}\int_{|y|\leq L}\frac{e^{-|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}|\phi_{Q^{2}}(y)u(y)|\mathrm{d}y+e^{c|x|}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}|\phi_{Qu}(y)Q(y)|\mathrm{d}y \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\ \int_{|y|\leq L}\frac{e^{|y|}|\phi_{Q^{2}}(y)|}{4\pi|x-y|}|u(y)|\mathrm{d}y+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-(1-c)|x-y|}}{4\pi|x-y|}|\phi_{Qu}(y)|\mathrm{d}y\leq C\|u\|_{L^{2}}\leq C. $$

Combining these estimates, we obtain

$$ \min\{M,e^{c|x|}\}|u(x)|\leq C+\frac{1}{2}\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{3}}\min\{M,e^{c|y|}\}|u(y)|. $$

Taking supremum in $x$ , we get

$$ \min\{M,e^{c|x|}\}|u(x)|\leq C,\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{3} $$

with $C>0$ independent of $M$ . Then letting $M\to+\infty$ gives the desired estimate.

For (2), using $Q\in\ker(L_{-})$ , we may choose $u$ so that $L_{-}u=f$ and $(u,\Lambda Q)=0$ . Here, we have used the fact that $(Q,\Lambda Q)\neq 0$ . Then Lemma 2.1 implies $(L_{-}u,u)\geq C^{-1}\|u\|_{H^{1}}^{2}$ . We then deduce $\|u\|_{L^{2}}\leq C$ similarly. The remaining proof is identical to (1). ∎

## 3. Approximate two-soliton solutions

In this section, we construct approximate two-soliton solutions to the Hartree equation (1.1) in Proposition 3.3 and prove quantified accuracy estimates for approximate solutions in Proposition 3.9. The strategy was introduced in [9] and was applied to multisolitons in [19]; our notation is closer to that of [19]. However, we make a few key modifications. First, we introduce a cutoff function in (3.12) when defining the dipole expansion. Second, we add an additional term in (3.16) and (3.17) when splitting the interaction error. Third, we introduce a quantitative version of admissible functions in Definition 3.5. These modifications lead to Proposition 3.4 and Proposition 3.9, which are new ingredients of this paper as mentioned in Section 1.

Let us introduce some notation. When given parameters $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}$ , we write

$$ \displaystyle P=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}),\quad g=(P,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}), \displaystyle g_{1}=(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1},\lambda_{1},\gamma_{1}),\quad g_{2}=(\alpha_{2},\beta_{2},\lambda_{2},\gamma_{2}), \displaystyle\alpha=\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1},\quad\beta=\beta_{2}-\beta_{1},\quad\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}),\quad r=|\alpha|. $$

We use similar notation for superscripted quantities. For a function $v$ , let

$$ g_{j}v(t,x)=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}v\Big(t,\frac{x-\alpha_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}\Big)e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x},\quad j=1,2. $$

Consider the $2$ -soliton

$$ u(t,x):=u_{1}+u_{2}:=g_{1}v_{1}+g_{2}v_{2}. $$

Then we have

$$ iu_{t}+\Delta u-\phi_{|u|^{2}}u=\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}E_{j}(t,y_{j})e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(u_{1}\overline{u_{2}})}u $$

with

$$ \displaystyle E_{j}(t,y_{j})= \displaystyle i\partial_{t}v_{j}+\lambda_{j}^{-2}\big(\Delta v_{j}-v_{j}-\phi_{|v_{j}|^{2}}v_{j}\big)-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j+1}^{2}}\phi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}\left(t,\frac{\lambda_{j}y_{j}}{\lambda_{j+1}}+\frac{(-1)^{j}\alpha}{\lambda_{j+1}}\right)v_{j} \displaystyle-i\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}\nabla v_{j}-i\frac{\dot{\lambda}_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}\Lambda v_{j}-\lambda_{j}\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot y_{j}v_{j}-\Big(\dot{\gamma}_{j}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}+\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot\alpha_{j}\Big)v_{j}, $$

where we set $y_{j}=\frac{x-\alpha_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}$ . Note that

$$ \frac{1}{\lambda_{j+1}^{2}}\phi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}\left(t,\frac{\lambda_{j}y_{j}}{\lambda_{j+1}}+\frac{(-1)^{j}\alpha}{\lambda_{j+1}}\right)=-\frac{1}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{|v_{j+1}(t,\xi)|^{2}}{|\lambda_{j}y_{j}+(-1)^{j}\alpha-\lambda_{j+1}\xi|}\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

To construct approximate solutions, we consider the Taylor expansion

$$ \frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)+O\left(\frac{|\zeta|^{N}}{|\alpha|^{N+1}}\right)\;\;\text{as}\;\;\zeta\to 0, $$

where $F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)$ is homogeneous of degree $-n$ in $\alpha$ and of degree $n-1$ in $\zeta$ . We can calculate the first few terms explicitly:

$$ F_{1}(\alpha,\zeta)=\frac{1}{|\alpha|},\quad F_{2}(\alpha,\zeta)=\frac{\alpha\cdot\zeta}{|\alpha|^{3}},\quad F_{3}(\alpha,\zeta)=\frac{1}{2|\alpha|^{5}}\big[3(\alpha\cdot\zeta)^{2}-|\alpha|^{2}|\zeta|^{2}\big]. $$

As in [19], we define

$$ \psi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}^{(n)}(t,y_{j})=-\frac{1}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|v_{j+1}(t,\xi)|^{2}F_{n}\big(\alpha,(-1)^{j}(\lambda_{j+1}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})\big)\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

When $v_{j+1}=Q$ , we denote $\psi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}^{(n)}$ by $\psi_{Q^{2},j+1}^{(n)}$ to indicate its dependence on $j$ .

Note that the Taylor expansion is not useful when $\zeta=(-1)^{j}(\lambda_{j+1}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})$ is large compared to $|\alpha|$ . In [9, 19], using the expansion for all $\zeta$ is harmless because one can first take $N$ large enough and then take $|\alpha|$ large enough, as $|\alpha(t)|\to\infty$ in the expansive case, thus absorbing the polynomial growth by the exponential decay. However, this is impossible in the elliptic case where $|\alpha|$ is bounded for a fixed trajectory. Our solution is to introduce a cutoff so that the approximation only captures small $\zeta$ . In practice, it is more convenient to let the cutoff function be a function of $y_{j}$ . Another subtle point is that we will need precise formulae for the first few terms of the approximation as in Proposition 3.4, so we do not want the cutoff to affect the first few terms. Therefore, we only apply the cutoff for $n>10$ , where the choice of $10$ is quite flexible: it can be any order above which explicit expressions for the approximation are not required.

More precisely, we fix a smooth function $\chi:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ such that $\chi(x)=1$ if $|x|\leq 1$ and $\chi(x)=0$ if $|x|\geq 2$ . Then we define

$$ \psi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}^{(n),L}(t,y_{j})=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\psi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}^{(n)}(t,y_{j}),&&n\leq 10,\\
&\psi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}^{(n)}(t,y_{j})\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L}),&&n>10,\end{aligned}\right. $$

and

$$ \phi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}^{(N),L}(t,y_{j}):=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\psi_{|v_{j+1}|^{2}}^{(n),L}(t,y_{j}), $$

where $L>0$ is a constant that will be specified later.

We shall allow $v_{j}$ to depend on $N$ , and we also assume $v_{j}$ depends on time only through the parameters $t\mapsto P(t)$ , which means $v_{j}(t,y_{j})=V_{j}^{(N)}(P(t),y_{j})$ for some $V_{j}^{(N)}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle R_{g}^{(N)}(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^{2}R_{j,g}^{(N)}(t,x):=\sum_{j=1}^{2}g_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}(P(t),x). $$

Let us omit the subscript $g$ of $R^{(N)}$ for now. We have

$$ \displaystyle i\partial_{t}R^{(N)}+\Delta R^{(N)}-\phi_{|R^{(N)}|^{2}}R^{(N)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}E_{j}^{(N)}(t,y_{j})e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}\Big(R_{1}^{(N)}\overline{R_{2}^{(N)}}\Big)}R^{(N)} \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}\left[\phi_{\left|V_{j+1}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}^{(N),L}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j+1}^{2}}\phi_{|V_{j+1}^{(N)}|^{2}}\left(P(t),\frac{\lambda_{j}y_{j}}{\lambda_{j+1}}+\frac{(-1)^{j}\alpha}{\lambda_{j+1}}\right)\right]V_{j}^{(N)}e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}, $$

where $E_{j}^{(N)}=\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}+S_{j}^{(N)}$ , with $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ collecting nonlinear errors and $S_{j}^{(N)}$ collecting modulation errors. Namely, we let

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}(t,y_{j})= \displaystyle\lambda_{j}^{-2}\Big(\Delta V_{j}^{(N)}-V_{j}^{(N)}-\phi_{\left|V_{j}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}V_{j}^{(N)}\Big)-\phi_{\left|V_{j+1}^{(N)}\right|^{2}}^{(N),L}V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle-i\frac{M_{j}^{(N)}}{\lambda_{j}}\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}-\lambda_{j}B_{j}^{(N)}\cdot y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle+i\Bigg[\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot 2\beta+\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\beta}\cdot\left(B_{2}^{(N)}-B_{1}^{(N)}\right)+\sum_{k=1}^{2}\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}M_{k}^{(N)}\Bigg] $$

and

$$ \displaystyle S_{j}^{(N)}(t,y_{j})= \displaystyle-i\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{j}-2\beta_{j}}{\lambda_{j}}\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}-\lambda_{j}\left(\dot{\beta}_{j}-B_{j}^{(N)}\right)\cdot y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}-i\frac{\dot{\lambda}_{j}-M_{j}^{(N)}}{\lambda_{j}}\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle-\Big(\dot{\gamma}_{j}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}+\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot\alpha_{j}-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}\Big)V_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle+i\Bigg[\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot\left(\dot{\alpha}-2\beta\right)+\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\beta}\cdot\left(\dot{\beta}-B_{2}^{(N)}+B_{1}^{(N)}\right)\Bigg] \displaystyle+i\sum_{k=1}^{2}\frac{\partial V_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\lambda_{k}}\left(\dot{\lambda}_{k}-M_{k}^{(N)}\right). $$

#### Remark 3.1.

This error expansion is almost the same as what was done in [9, 19], except that we add an additional term $-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}V_{j}^{(N)}$ in (3.16) and a corresponding term in (3.17). We will call this term an interaction shift since it modifies the equation for $\gamma_{j}$ when we later impose the condition $S_{j}^{(N)}=0$ . This is reflected in both Theorem 1 and Proposition 5.1.

The interaction shift cancels the first-order interaction term, and, with the aid of spherical harmonics, leads to further higher-order cancellations. The first-order calculation in the proof of Proposition 3.4, given in Section 4, contains the details of this cancellation.

The interaction shift also appears in the Lagrangian formulation of the effective dynamics. In this derivation, the same quantity enters the equation for $\gamma_{j}$ , providing an alternative interpretation of the term introduced above. Since the calculation is lengthy and plays no role in the proof, we omit the details.

We recall the following definition of admissible functions from [9, 19]. These functions have good decay in both $|\alpha|$ and $x$ .

#### Definition 3.2 (Admissible functions).

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ .

(1) Define $S_{n}$ to be the set of functions $\sigma:(\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{C}$ of the form

$$ \sigma(\alpha,\beta,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})=\sum z_{s,t,p,q}|\alpha|^{-n-|s|}\alpha^{s}\beta^{t}\lambda_{1}^{p}\lambda_{2}^{q}, $$

where the sum is finite, $s,t\in\mathbb{N}^{3}$ , $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $z_{s,t,p,q}\in\mathbb{C}$ .

(2) We say a function $u:(\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}$ is admissible of degree $n$ if it is of the form

$$ u(\alpha,\beta,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},x)=\sum z_{s,t,p,q}|\alpha|^{-n-|s|}\alpha^{s}\beta^{t}\lambda_{1}^{p}\lambda_{2}^{q}f_{s,t,p,q}(x), $$

where the sum is finite, $s,t\in\mathbb{N}^{3}$ , $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$ and

$$ z_{s,t,p,q}\in\mathbb{C};\quad|\nabla^{k}f_{s,t,p,q}(x)|\leq C_{k,s,t,p,q}e^{-c_{k,s,t,p,q}|x|},\;\;\forall k\in\mathbb{N},\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

(3) We say $u:(\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}$ is admissible of degree $\geq n$ if $u$ is a finite sum of functions of degree $n^{\prime}$ with $n^{\prime}\geq n$ .

Approximate solutions can then be constructed as follows.

#### Proposition 3.3.

There exist $b_{j}^{(n)},m_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n}$ that are real-valued and $T_{j}^{(n)}$ that is admissible of degree $n$ for $n\geq 1$ , $j=1,2$ such that: for any $N\geq 1$ , if we let

$$ \displaystyle V_{j}^{(N)}(\alpha,\beta,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},y_{j})=Q(y_{j})+\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{j}^{(n)}(\alpha,\beta,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},y_{j}), \displaystyle M_{j}^{(N)}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}m_{j}^{(n)}\quad\text{and}\quad B_{j}^{(N)}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}b_{j}^{(n)}, $$

then $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ defined by (3.16) is admissible of degree $\geq N+1$ .

#### Proof.

The proof is identical to [9, Proposition 2.3] or [19, Proposition 2.4], despite the additional term $-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}V_{j}^{(N)}$ and the cutoff (3.12). The construction can be carried out in the same way. We will only provide a sketch and explain how to determine $m_{j}^{(n)},b_{j}^{(n)}$ and $T_{j}^{(n)}$ .

Let $\hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ denote the terms in $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ that are of degree $-N-1$ in $\alpha$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}= \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}^{-2}\sum_{k+l+m=N+1}\phi_{\mathrm{Re}\big(T_{j}^{(k)}\overline{T_{j}^{(l)}}\big)}T_{j}^{(m)}-\sum_{k+l+m+n=N+1}\psi^{(n),L}_{\mathrm{Re}\big(T_{j+1}^{(k)}\overline{T_{j+1}^{(l)}}\big)}T_{j}^{(m)} \displaystyle-\frac{i}{\lambda_{j}}\sum_{m+n=N+1}m_{j}^{(n)}\Lambda T_{j}^{(m)}-\lambda_{j}\sum_{m+n=N+1}b_{j}^{(n)}\cdot y_{j}T_{j}^{(m)}-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}T_{j}^{(N)} \displaystyle+i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(N)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot 2\beta+i\sum_{m+n=N+1}\bigg[\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(m)}}{\partial\beta}\cdot\Big(b_{2}^{(n)}-b_{1}^{(n)}\Big)+\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(m)}}{\partial\lambda_{1}}m_{1}^{(n)}+\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(m)}}{\partial\lambda_{2}}m_{2}^{(n)}\bigg], $$

where the indices $k,l,m$ range from $0$ to $N$ , $n$ ranges from $1$ to $N$ , and we set $T_{j}^{(0)}=Q$ .

Then we choose the $(N+1)$ -th order terms to cancel $\hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ . We let $b_{j}^{(N+1)}$ , $m_{j}^{(N+1)}$ satisfy

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &\Big(\lambda_{j}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q+\psi_{Q^{2},j+1}^{(N+1),L}Q-\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\nabla Q\Big)=0,\\
&\left(m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q-\lambda_{j}\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},Q\right)=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$

and then solve $T_{j}^{(N+1)}$ from

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &L_{+}\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(N+1)}=-\lambda_{j}^{3}b_{j}^{(N+1)}\cdot y_{j}Q-\lambda_{j}^{2}\psi_{Q^{2},j+1}^{(N+1),L}Q+\lambda_{j}^{2}\mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)},\\
&L_{-}\mathrm{Im}\ T_{j}^{(N+1)}=-\lambda_{j}m_{j}^{(N+1)}\Lambda Q+\lambda_{j}^{2}\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Here, the orthogonality condition (3.22) ensures that (3.23) is solvable according to Lemma 2.2. Then the proposition can be proved by induction. See [19] for more details. ∎

Using (3.21), (3.22) and (3.23), we can compute the first few terms of $B_{j}^{(N)}$ , $M_{j}^{(N)}$ and $T_{j}^{(N)}$ . These terms turn out to be unexpectedly simple.

#### Proposition 3.4.

We have $T_{j}^{(1)}=T_{j}^{(2)}=0$ , $b_{j}^{(2)}=\frac{(-1)^{j-1}\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{\alpha}{|\alpha|^{3}}$ and

$$ b_{j}^{(n)}=0\;\;\text{for}\;\;1\leq n\leq 6,\;n\neq 2;\quad m_{j}^{(n)}=0\;\;\text{for}\;\;1\leq n\leq 6. $$

The significance of this result will become clear in Section 4 when we prove Proposition 4.2, so we postpone its proof to the next section. We would like to emphasize that the key reason this holds is the interaction shift (see Remark 3.1).

The next step is to prove the accuracy of approximate solutions similar to [9, Proposition 2.7] or [19, Proposition 2.6]. However, in those papers, the dependence of the constants on $N$ is not tracked, while this information is needed in this paper. For this purpose, we need to define a more quantitative version of admissible functions and show quantitative estimates for the data constructed above.

#### Definition 3.5 (Quantified admissible functions).

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ , $A>0$ and $c>0$ .

(1) Define $S_{n}(A)$ to be the set of functions

$$ \sigma:(\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{C} $$

of the form

$$ \sigma(\alpha,\beta,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})=\sum z_{s,t,p,q}|\alpha|^{-n-|s|}\alpha^{s}\beta^{t}\lambda_{1}^{p}\lambda_{2}^{q}, $$

where the summation is over

$$ s\in\mathbb{N}^{3},\;|s|\leq n;\quad t\in\mathbb{N}^{3},\;|t|\leq n;\quad p\in\mathbb{Z},\;|p|\leq 5n;\quad q\in\mathbb{Z},\;|q|\leq 5n, $$

and

$$ z_{s,t,p,q}\in\mathbb{C},\quad\sum|z_{s,t,p,q}|\leq A. $$

(2) Define $\mathcal{S}_{n}(A,c)$ to be the set of functions

$$ u:(\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C} $$

of the form

$$ u(\alpha,\beta,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},x)=\sum z_{s,t,p,q}|\alpha|^{-n-|s|}\alpha^{s}\beta^{t}\lambda_{1}^{p}\lambda_{2}^{q}f_{s,t,p,q}(x), $$

where the summation is over (3.27), with (3.20) being satisfied, and

$$ \sum|z_{s,t,p,q}|\leq A,\quad|f_{s,t,p,q}(x)|\leq e^{-c|x|},\;\;\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

The following lemma gives quantitative bounds for the closure properties of admissible functions. We remark that (3) below heavily relies on (3.12).

#### Lemma 3.6.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ and $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ . Assume $u\in\mathcal{S}_{m}(A,c_{1})$ and $v\in\mathcal{S}_{n}(B,c_{2})$ . Then

- (1) $uv\in\mathcal{S}_{m+n}(AB,c_{1}+c_{2})$ ;

- (2) $\phi_{u}v\in\mathcal{S}_{m+n}(CAB,c_{2})$ for some $C>0$ depending only on $c_{1}$ ;

- (3) If $0<\epsilon\ll 1$ , $k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ and $k\leq L$ , then $\psi_{u}^{(k),L}v\in\mathcal{S}_{m+n+k}(C^{k}L^{k-1}AB,c_{2}-\epsilon L^{-1}\big)$ for some $C>0$ depending only on $c_{1}$ and $\epsilon$ .

- (4) If $0<\epsilon\ll 1$ , $k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ and $k\leq L^{\frac{1}{3}}$ , then $\psi_{u}^{(k),L}v\in\mathcal{S}_{m+n+k}(C^{k}L^{\frac{2(k-1)}{3}}AB,c_{2}-\epsilon L^{-\frac{1}{3}}\big)$ for some $C>0$ depending only on $c_{1}$ and $\epsilon$ .

#### Proof.

The proof of (1) and (2) is standard. Then we prove (3). By linearity, we may assume $u$ and $v$ both consist of one term and $A=B=1$ . Namely,

$$ u=|\alpha|^{-m-|s_{1}|}\alpha^{s_{1}}\beta^{t_{1}}\lambda_{1}^{p_{1}}\lambda_{2}^{q_{1}}f_{s_{1},t_{1},p_{1},q_{1}}(x),\quad v=|\alpha|^{-n-|s_{2}|}\alpha^{s_{2}}\beta^{t_{2}}\lambda_{1}^{p_{2}}\lambda_{2}^{q_{2}}f_{s_{2},t_{2},p_{2},q_{2}}(x) $$

with

$$ |f_{s_{1},t_{1},p_{1},q_{1}}(x)|\leq e^{-c_{1}|x|},\quad|f_{s_{2},t_{2},p_{2},q_{2}}(x)|\leq e^{-c_{2}|x|}. $$

Since the Taylor series of the power function $|\alpha-\zeta|^{-1}$ has a finite radius of convergence, there is a universal constant $C>0$ such that $|F_{k}(\alpha,\zeta)|\leq C^{k}|\alpha|^{-k}|\zeta|^{k-1}$ for all $k\geq 1$ . We write

$$ F_{k}(\alpha,\zeta)=\sum c_{s,l}|\alpha|^{-k-|s|}\alpha^{s}\zeta^{l}, $$

where the summation is over $s,l\in\mathbb{N}^{3}$ , $|s|\leq k$ , $|l|=k-1$ . We have $\sum|c_{s,l}|\leq C^{k}$ .

If $k>10$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{u}^{(k),L}v(y_{j}) \displaystyle=\int f_{s_{1},t_{1},p_{1},q_{1}}(\xi)F_{k}\big(\alpha,(-1)^{j}(\lambda_{j+1}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})\big)\mathrm{d}\xi\cdot\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L}) \displaystyle\cdot|\alpha|^{-m-n-|s_{1}|-|s_{2}|}\alpha^{s_{1}+s_{2}}\beta^{t_{1}+t_{2}}\lambda_{1}^{p_{1}+p_{2}}\lambda_{2}^{q_{1}+q_{2}}f_{s_{2},t_{2},p_{2},q_{2}}(y_{j}) \displaystyle=\sum\int f_{s_{1},t_{1},p_{1},q_{1}}(\xi)(\lambda_{j+1}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})^{l}\mathrm{d}\xi\cdot c_{s,l}\cdot(-1)^{j(k-1)}\cdot\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L}) \displaystyle\cdot|\alpha|^{-m-n-k-|s_{1}|-|s_{2}|-|s|}\alpha^{s_{1}+s_{2}+s}\beta^{t_{1}+t_{2}}\lambda_{1}^{p_{1}+p_{2}}\lambda_{2}^{q_{1}+q_{2}}f_{s_{2},t_{2},p_{2},q_{2}}(y_{j}). $$

We expand $(\lambda_{j+1}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})^{l}$ in the integrand. For any $0\leq p\leq|l|=k-1$ , we have

$$ \int|f_{s_{1},t_{1},p_{1},q_{1}}(\xi)||\xi|^{p}\mathrm{d}\xi\leq C^{p}p!,\quad C=C(c_{1})>0, $$

and $|y_{j}|^{k-p-1}\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L})\leq(2L)^{k-p-1}$ . It follows that $\psi_{u}^{(k),L}v\in\mathcal{S}_{m+n+k}(\tilde{A},c_{2})$ , where

$$ \tilde{A}\leq C^{k}\sum_{p=0}^{k-1}p!L^{k-p-1}\leq C^{k}(k+L)^{k-1}. $$

Then we obtain (3) since $k\leq L$ .

If $k\leq 10$ , then there is no cutoff term $\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L})$ in (3.35). By pairing $|y_{j}|^{k-p-1}$ with $e^{-\epsilon L^{-1}|y_{j}|}$ , we deduce that $\psi_{u}^{(k),L}v\in\mathcal{S}_{m+n+k}(\tilde{B},c_{2}-\epsilon L^{-1})$ , where

$$ \tilde{B}\leq C^{k}\sum_{p=0}^{k-1}p!\sup\big(|y_{j}|^{k-p-1}e^{-\epsilon L^{-1}|y_{j}|}\big)\leq C^{k}\sum_{p=0}^{k-1}p!L^{k-p-1}\sup\big((1+|y_{j}|)^{10}e^{-|y_{j}|}\big). $$

This proves (3) in the case $k\leq 10$ as well. Thus (3) is proved.

The proof of (4) is very similar. We proceed until (3.35) but ignore $\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L})$ anyway. This time, we pair $|y_{j}|^{k-p-1}$ with $e^{-\epsilon L^{-\frac{1}{3}}|y_{j}|}$ . It follows that $\psi_{u}^{(k),L}v\in\mathcal{S}_{m+n+k}(\tilde{C},c_{2}-\epsilon L^{-\frac{1}{3}})$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{C} \displaystyle\leq C^{k}\sum_{p=0}^{k-1}p!\sup\big(|y_{j}|^{k-p-1}e^{-\epsilon L^{-\frac{1}{3}}|y_{j}|}\big)\leq C^{k}\sum_{p=0}^{k-1}p!L^{\frac{k-p-1}{3}}\sup\big(|y_{j}|^{k-p-1}e^{-|y_{j}|}\big) \displaystyle\leq C^{k}\sum_{p=0}^{k-1}p!L^{\frac{2(k-p-1)}{3}}\leq C^{k}L^{\frac{2(k-1)}{3}}, $$

where we have used $k\leq L^{\frac{1}{3}}$ in the second line. This concludes the proof. ∎

We next show $b_{j}^{(n)},m_{j}^{(n)}$ and $T_{j}^{(n)}$ are elements of the quantified admissible function spaces. We can also describe their size in terms of $n$ .

#### Lemma 3.7.

Let $b_{j}^{(n)},m_{j}^{(n)}$ and $T_{j}^{(n)}$ be as defined in Proposition 3.3. There are universal constants $C,c>0$ such that for any $L>1$ , one has

$$ b_{j}^{(n)},m_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n}(C^{n}L^{n-1}),\quad T_{j}^{(n)}\in\mathcal{S}_{n}(C^{n}L^{n-1},c),\quad\forall 1\leq n\leq[L],\;j=1,2. $$

#### Proof.

We take $c_{0}$ to be the constant in Lemma 2.2. By the proof of Lemma 2.2, we know that there is $A_{0}>0$ such that $Q(x)\leq A_{0}e^{-c_{0}|x|}$ .

We first prove by induction that there exists $A_{n}>0$ for $1\leq n\leq[L]$ such that

$$ m_{j}^{(n)},b_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n}(A_{n}),\quad T_{j}^{(n)}\in\mathcal{S}_{n}(A_{n},c_{0}-c_{0}(2L)^{-1}n),\quad\forall 1\leq n\leq[L],\;j=1,2. $$

Suppose (3.42) holds for $1\leq n\leq N$ , where $N\leq[L]-1$ . Recall $\hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ is defined by (3.21). By Lemma 3.6 and (3.27), we have $\hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}\in\mathcal{S}_{N+1}(\tilde{A}_{N+1},c_{0}-c_{0}(2L)^{-1}(N+1))$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{A}_{N+1} \displaystyle=C_{0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+l+m=N+1\\
0\leq k,l,m\leq N\end{subarray}}A_{k}A_{l}A_{m}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+l+m+n=N+1\\
0\leq k,l,m\leq N,\ 1\leq n\leq N+1\end{subarray}}C_{0}^{n}L^{n-1}A_{k}A_{l}A_{m} \displaystyle\quad+C_{0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m+n=N+1\\
1\leq m,n\leq N\end{subarray}}mA_{m}A_{n}, $$

and $C_{0}>0$ is a universal constant large enough. In particular, we have used $N+1\leq[L]$ and applied Lemma 3.6 (3) with $c_{2}=c_{0}-c_{0}(2L)^{-1}N$ , $\epsilon=c_{0}/2$ . We combine the first two sums in $\tilde{A}_{N+1}$ and define a more convenient quantity

$$ A_{N+1}=C_{0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+l+m+n=N+1\\
0\leq k,l,m\leq N,\ 0\leq n\leq N+1\end{subarray}}C_{0}^{n}L^{(n-1)_{+}}A_{k}A_{l}A_{m}+C_{0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m+n=N+1\\
1\leq m,n\leq N\end{subarray}}LA_{m}A_{n}, $$

where $(n-1)_{+}=\max\{n-1,0\}$ . Since $A_{N+1}\geq\tilde{A}_{N+1}$ , we still have

$$ \hat{E}_{j}^{(N)}\in\mathcal{S}_{N+1}(A_{N+1},c_{0}-c_{0}(2L)^{-1}(N+1)). $$

Then using (3.22), (3.23) and Lemma 2.2, we obtain (3.42) for $n=N+1$ , with possibly a larger $C_{0}$ in (3.45). Note that (3.27) can be checked by counting the additional powers of $\alpha,\beta,\lambda_{j}$ .

Therefore, we have proved (3.42) with $\{A_{n}\}$ defined by (3.45). Since $c_{0}-c_{0}(2L)^{-1}n\geq\frac{c_{0}}{2}$ , we may take $c=\frac{c_{0}}{2}$ and it remains to prove

$$ A_{n}\leq C^{n}L^{n-1},\quad\forall 1\leq n\leq[L]. $$

Let $B_{n}=C_{0}^{-n}L^{-(n-1)_{+}}A_{n}$ for $n\geq 0$ . In the first summation in (3.45), since $k,l,m,n$ cannot all be $0$ , one has $(k-1)_{+}+(l-1)_{+}+(m-1)_{+}+(n-1)_{+}\leq N$ . Therefore, we obtain

$$ A_{N+1}\leq C_{0}^{N+2}L^{N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+l+m+n=N+1\\
0\leq k,l,m\leq N,\ 0\leq n\leq N+1\end{subarray}}B_{k}B_{l}B_{m}+C_{0}^{N+2}L^{N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m+n=N+1\\
1\leq m,n\leq N\end{subarray}}B_{m}B_{n}, $$

and thus

$$ B_{N+1}\leq 2C_{0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+l+m\leq N+1\\
0\leq k,l,m\leq N\end{subarray}}B_{k}B_{l}B_{m}. $$

We prove in Appendix A that this implies $B_{n}\leq C^{n}$ , which completes the proof. ∎

#### Remark 3.8.

In the induction step of the above proof, if we use Lemma 3.6 (4) instead of (3), then we can prove

$$ b_{j}^{(n)},m_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n}(C^{n}L^{\frac{2(n-1)}{3}}),\quad T_{j}^{(n)}\in\mathcal{S}_{n}(C^{n}L^{\frac{2(n-1)}{3}},c),\quad\forall 1\leq n\leq[L^{\frac{1}{3}}],\;j=1,2. $$

We conclude this section with the following estimates for the accuracy of the approximate solution. It is important that the constants $c_{0},C_{0}$ do not depend on $N$ .

#### Proposition 3.9.

For $K>1$ , there exist $\bar{r}_{0}>0$ , $\eta>0$ and $c_{0},C_{0}>0$ such that the following is true. Assume $r_{0}>\bar{r}_{0}$ , $N\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ , $\frac{1}{2}\eta r_{0}\leq N\leq L\leq\eta r_{0}$ and $P(t)$ satisfies

$$ |\alpha|\geq r_{0},\quad|\beta|\leq K,\quad K^{-1}\leq\lambda_{j}\leq K. $$

- (1) Let $V_{j}^{(N)}$ , $M_{j}^{(N)}$ and $B_{j}^{(N)}$ be as in Proposition 3.3. Then (3.52)

$$ |B_{j}^{(N)}-b_{j}^{(2)}|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-7},\quad|M_{j}^{(N)}|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-7}, $$

(3.53)

$$ |V_{j}^{(N)}-Q|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-3}e^{-c_{0}|y_{j}|}. $$

- (2) Let $R_{g}^{(N)}$ be defined by (3.14), and (3.54)

$$ \Psi^{(N)}=i\partial_{t}R_{g}^{(N)}+\Delta R_{g}^{(N)}-\phi_{|R_{g}^{(N)}|^{2}}R_{g}^{(N)}-\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}S_{j}^{(N)}e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}. $$

Then (3.55)

$$ |\Psi^{(N)}(t,x)|\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\max\limits_{j}e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}. $$

#### Remark 3.10.

We give a heuristic explanation of the range of $N$ and $L$ .

The Taylor expansion of $\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}$ is valid if $|\zeta|<|\alpha|$ . In (3.12), we roughly have $|y_{j}|\sim|\zeta|$ , so the cutoff threshold $L$ has size $r_{0}$ .

From the last term in the expression of $\tilde{A}_{N+1}$ in the proof of Lemma 3.7, we see $A_{n}$ grows at least like $n!$ , meaning that $|b_{j}^{(n)}|\leq n!r_{0}^{-n}$ is the best bound one may expect for all $n$ . By Stirling’s formula, the minimum of $n!r_{0}^{-n}$ is attained near $n\sim r_{0}$ , so the approximation order $N$ also has size $r_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

In the proof, we let $c_{0},C_{0}$ denote positive constants depending only on $K$ , where $c_{0}$ is small and $C_{0}$ is large. These constants may change from line to line. Recall we set $r=|\alpha|$ .

(1) By ignoring $L$ completely and simply using $m_{j}^{(n)}\in S_{n}$ , we have $\sum_{n=7}^{20}|m_{j}^{(n)}|\leq C_{0}r^{-7}$ . Recall that from the definition of $S_{n}(A)$ , we have

$$ \sigma\in S_{n}(A)\implies|\sigma(\alpha,\beta,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})|\leq C_{0}^{n}Ar^{-n}\text{ when \eqref{eq rough estimate on parameters} holds}. $$

Then, using (3.50) and $L\leq\eta r_{0}$ with $\eta$ small enough, we get

$$ \sum_{21\leq n\leq L^{1/3}}|m_{j}^{(n)}|\leq\sum_{21\leq n\leq L^{1/3}}C_{0}^{n}L^{\frac{2n}{3}}r^{-n}\leq\sum_{21\leq n\leq L^{1/3}}(C_{0}\eta)^{n}r^{-7}\leq C_{0}r^{-7}. $$

By Lemma 3.7 and taking $\eta$ small enough as well, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{L^{1/3}<n\leq N}|m_{j}^{(n)}|\leq\sum_{L^{1/3}<n\leq N}C_{0}^{n}L^{n}r^{-n}\leq(C_{0}\eta)^{L^{\frac{1}{3}}}\leq e^{-L^{\frac{1}{3}}}. $$

Then we get $|M_{j}^{(N)}|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-7}$ by adding up these inequalities and using Proposition 3.4. The estimates for $B_{j}^{(N)}$ and $V_{j}^{(N)}$ are proved similarly.

(2) By (3.15), we have (omitting the superscript $N$ and the subscript $g$ for simplicity)

$$ \displaystyle\Psi \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}\tilde{E}_{j}(t,y_{j})e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(R_{1}\overline{R_{2}})}R \displaystyle+\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}\left[\phi_{\left|V_{j+1}\right|^{2}}^{(N),L}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j+1}^{2}}\phi_{|V_{j+1}|^{2}}\left(P(t),\frac{\lambda_{j}y_{j}}{\lambda_{j+1}}+\frac{(-1)^{j}\alpha}{\lambda_{j+1}}\right)\right]V_{j}e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}. $$

The second term on the first line is bounded by the right-hand side of (3.55) using (3.53).

For the first term on the first line, using (3.16) and Lemma 3.7, we have

$$ |\tilde{E}_{j}|\leq\sum_{n=N+1}^{4N+4}C_{0}^{n}L^{n}r^{-n}e^{-c_{0}|y_{j}|}\leq\sum_{n=N+1}^{4N+4}(C_{0}\eta)^{n}e^{-c_{0}|y_{j}|}\leq e^{-N}e^{-c_{0}|y_{j}|}, $$

provided $\eta$ is small enough. Then we have $|\tilde{E}_{j}|\leq e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}e^{-c_{0}|y_{j}|}$ since $N\geq\frac{1}{2}\eta r_{0}$ .

It remains to consider the second line. We set $\zeta=(-1)^{j}(\lambda_{j+1}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\quad\ \phi_{\left|V_{j+1}\right|^{2}}^{(N),L}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j+1}^{2}}\phi_{|V_{j+1}|^{2}}\left(\frac{\lambda_{j}y_{j}}{\lambda_{j+1}}+\frac{(-1)^{j}\alpha}{\lambda_{j+1}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\int|V_{j+1}(\xi)|^{2}\bigg(\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}-\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)\bigg)\mathrm{d}\xi+\sum_{n=11}^{N}\psi^{(n)}_{|V_{j+1}|^{2}}\big(1-\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L})\big). $$

We separate the integral into $I_{1}+I_{2}$ , where

$$ I_{1}=\int_{\{|\zeta|\leq\frac{1}{2}r\}}|V_{j+1}(\xi)|^{2}\bigg(\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}-\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)\bigg)\mathrm{d}\xi $$

and

$$ I_{2}=\int_{\{|\zeta|\geq\frac{1}{2}r\}}|V_{j+1}(\xi)|^{2}\bigg(\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}-\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)\bigg)\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

If $|\zeta|\leq\frac{1}{2}r$ , then the power series $\sum F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)$ converges, which implies

$$ \bigg|\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}-\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)\bigg|\leq C_{0}^{N}\frac{|\zeta|^{N}}{r^{N+1}}. $$

By (3.53), there exists $c_{1}>0$ depending on $K$ such that $|V_{j+1}(\xi)|\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{1}|\xi|}$ . Using

$$ |\xi|\geq(2K)^{-1}|\xi|\geq\frac{1}{2}K^{-2}|\zeta|-\frac{1}{2}|y_{j}| $$

and

$$ \int e^{-|x|}|x|^{N}\mathrm{d}x\leq C_{0}^{N}N! $$

we obtain

$$ \displaystyle|I_{1}| \displaystyle\leq\frac{C_{0}^{N}}{r^{N+1}}\int e^{-c_{1}|\xi|}|\zeta|^{N}\mathrm{d}\xi\leq\frac{C_{0}^{N}}{r^{N+1}}e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}\int e^{-\frac{c_{1}}{2K^{2}}|\zeta|}|\zeta|^{N}\mathrm{d}\xi\leq\frac{C_{0}^{N}N!}{r^{N+1}}e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}. $$

Then from $\frac{1}{2}\eta r_{0}\leq N\leq\eta r_{0}$ , taking $\eta$ small enough, we get

$$ |I_{1}|\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}. $$

If $|\zeta|\geq\frac{1}{2}r$ , then we use the crude estimate

$$ \bigg|\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}-\sum_{n=1}^{N}F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)\bigg|\leq\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}+C_{0}^{N}\frac{|2\zeta|^{N}}{r^{N}}. $$

The contribution of the second term is estimated as $I_{1}$ . For the first term $\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}$ , using

$$ |\xi|\geq\frac{1}{2}K^{-2}|\zeta|-\frac{1}{2}|y_{j}|\geq\frac{1}{8}K^{-2}r+\frac{1}{4}K^{-2}|\zeta|-\frac{1}{2}|y_{j}| $$

and integrability of $e^{-|x|}\frac{1}{|\alpha-x|}$ , we have

$$ \int_{\{|\zeta|\geq\frac{1}{2}r\}}|V_{j+1}(\xi)|^{2}\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}\mathrm{d}\xi\leq e^{-\frac{c_{1}}{8K^{2}}r}e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}\int e^{-\frac{c_{1}}{4K^{2}}|\zeta|}\frac{1}{|\alpha-\zeta|}\mathrm{d}\xi\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r}e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}. $$

We thus derive

$$ |I_{2}|\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}. $$

Finally, since $|F_{n}(\alpha,\zeta)|\leq C^{n}|\alpha|^{-n}|\zeta|^{n-1}$ , by similar estimates as for $I_{1}$ , we have

$$ \big|\psi^{(n)}_{|V_{j+1}|^{2}}(y_{j})\big|\leq\frac{C_{0}^{n}n!}{r^{n}}e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}\leq e^{-n}e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}\;\;\text{for}\;\;n\leq N, $$

provided $\eta$ is small enough. Then using $L\geq\frac{1}{2}\eta r_{0}$ , we obtain

$$ \sum_{n=11}^{N}\Big|\psi^{(n)}_{|V_{j+1}|^{2}}\big(1-\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L})\big)\Big|\leq\big(1-\chi(\frac{y_{j}}{L})\big)e^{\frac{1}{2}c_{1}|y_{j}|}\leq e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}e^{\frac{2}{3}c_{1}|y_{j}|}. $$

With all the above estimates as well as $|V_{j}(y_{j})|\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{1}|y_{j}|}$ , we deduce (3.55). ∎

## 4. Stability of the approximate center dynamics

In this section, we study the $N$ -th order approximation of the $2$ -body problem

$$ \dot{\alpha}_{j}=2\beta_{j},\quad\dot{\beta}_{j}=B_{j}^{(N)},\quad\dot{\lambda}_{j}=M_{j}^{(N)},\quad j=1,2. $$

where $B_{j}^{(N)}$ and $M_{j}^{(N)}$ are as in Proposition 3.3. If we can find a solution to this, then after solving $\gamma_{j}$ from

$$ \dot{\gamma}_{j}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}-|\beta_{j}|^{2}-\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot\alpha_{j}+\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}, $$

we will be able to eliminate the modulation error $S_{j}^{(N)}$ .

Our goal is to show that on a certain time scale, the solution to (4.1) remains close to the solution to (1.9). Note that Proposition 3.4 is an essential input for stability as it implies that the approximate acceleration differs from the Kepler acceleration only at order $|\alpha|^{-7}$ . For this reason, we provide the proof of Proposition 3.4 now.

First, since we only care about $n\leq 6$ , by (3.12), we always have $\psi^{(n),L}=\psi^{(n)}$ and the cutoff function $\chi$ is not involved.

Before carrying out the calculation, we need some preliminary facts. As in [6, Lemma 4.2], we have $\Delta_{x}F_{n}(\alpha,x)=0$ . This is because $F_{n}$ comes from the Taylor expansion of a harmonic function. This leads us to consider spherical harmonics; for reference, see [1].

For $l\geq 0$ , let $\mathcal{Y}_{l}=\left\{P|_{S^{2}}\ \big|\ P\text{ is homogeneous of degree }l\text{ and }\Delta P=0\right\}$ and

$$ \mathcal{H}_{l}=L^{2}\big((0,+\infty),r^{2}\mathrm{d}r\big)\otimes\mathcal{Y}_{l}, $$

which is the $l$ -th spherical harmonic subspace of $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ . The following properties will be useful:

- (a) $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})=\bigoplus_{l=0}^{\infty}\mathcal{H}_{l}$ , and $\mathcal{H}_{m}\perp\mathcal{H}_{n}$ whenever $m\neq n$ .

- (b) If $m<n$ , then $\mathcal{H}_{m}\cdot\mathcal{H}_{n}\cap L^{2}\subset\mathcal{H}_{n-m}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{n-m+2}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathcal{H}_{m+n}$ .

Property (a) implies that components in $\mathcal{H}_{l},\ l\geq 2$ do not affect $b_{j}^{(n)}$ and $m_{j}^{(n)}$ since $\nabla Q\in\mathcal{H}_{1}$ and $Q\in\mathcal{H}_{0}$ . It also gives some useful cancellation in our calculation. Property (b) will help us project terms in (3.21) into the spaces $\mathcal{H}_{l}$ .

We can give more information on $\psi^{(n)}$ . Assume $f\in\mathcal{H}_{l}$ and $f$ decays exponentially. Recall

$$ \psi_{f,j+1}^{(n)}(y_{j})=-\frac{1}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\int f(\xi)F_{n}\big(\alpha,(-1)^{j}(\lambda_{j+1}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})\big)\mathrm{d}\xi. $$

Note $F_{n}\in\mathcal{H}_{n-1}$ because $F_{n}\not\in L^{2}$ . But $F_{n}\in\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{n-1}$ for $n\geq 1$ , where

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{l}=\left\{f:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}\ \big|\ \forall\epsilon>0,e^{-\epsilon|\cdot|}f(\cdot)\in\mathcal{H}_{l}\right\}. $$

Take $0<\epsilon\ll 1$ so that $e^{\epsilon|\xi|}f(\xi)$ is still in $\mathcal{H}_{l}$ . For each $y_{j}$ , we have

$$ e^{-\epsilon|\xi|}F_{n}\big(\alpha,(-1)^{j}(\lambda_{j+1}\xi-\lambda_{j}y_{j})\big)\in\mathcal{H}_{0}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathcal{H}_{n-1}\quad(\text{in }\xi), $$

and the $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ -component is homogeneous of degree $n-k-1$ in $y_{j}$ . By Property (a), we deduce

$$ \psi_{f,j+1}^{(n)}(y_{j})\left\{\begin{aligned} &=0,&&n\leq l,\\
&\in\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{n-l-1},&&n>l.\end{aligned}\right. $$

In particular, we have $\psi_{Q^{2},j+1}^{(N+1)}\in\tilde{\mathcal{H}}_{N}$ and thus $\psi_{Q^{2},j+1}^{(N+1)}Q\in\mathcal{H}_{N}$ . Then Property (a) gives

$$ \big(\psi^{(N+1)}_{Q^{2},j+1}Q,\nabla Q\big)=0,\quad\forall N\geq 2. $$

Finally, note that $L_{\pm}:D(L_{\pm})\cap\mathcal{H}_{l}\to\mathcal{H}_{l}$ . In Lemma 2.2, if we have $f\in\mathcal{H}_{l}$ , then the inverse $u$ can also be chosen in $\mathcal{H}_{l}$ . We will use this choice when solving $T_{j}^{(n)}$ from (3.23).

#### Proof of Proposition 3.4.

With the convention that $V_{j}^{(0)}=T_{j}^{(0)}=Q$ , we can define $\tilde{E}_{j}^{(N)}$ for $N=0$ . Then (3.21), (3.22) and (3.23) are valid for all $N\geq 0$ .

1st order: Using (3.21), we have

$$ \hat{E}_{j}^{(0)}=-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}Q. $$

We compute directly $\psi_{Q^{2},j+1}^{(1)}=-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}$ . Then using (3.22), we get

$$ b_{j}^{(1)}=0,\quad m_{j}^{(1)}=0 $$

and thus (3.23) yields

$$ T_{j}^{(1)}=0. $$

We emphasize that this is the place where the interaction shift $-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}V_{j}^{(N)}$ in (3.16) is useful. It cancels $\psi_{Q^{2},j+1}^{(1)}Q$ when $N=0$ , which yields $T_{j}^{(1)}=0$ .

2nd order: Then we have $\hat{E}_{j}^{(1)}=0$ . We compute directly

$$ \psi_{Q^{2},j+1}^{(2)}=(-1)^{j}\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lambda_{j}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{\alpha\cdot y_{j}}{|\alpha|^{3}}. $$

Then using (3.22), we get

$$ b_{j}^{(2)}=\frac{(-1)^{j-1}\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{\alpha}{|\alpha|^{3}},\quad m_{j}^{(2)}=0 $$

and thus (3.23) yields

$$ T_{j}^{(2)}=0. $$

For higher orders, we do not compute the explicit formula of $T_{j}^{(n)}$ . Instead, we use properties of spherical harmonics to determine which $\mathcal{H}_{l}$ -component of $T_{j}^{(n)}$ is nonzero. This information will already be enough for us to obtain $b_{j}^{(n)}$ and $m_{j}^{(n)}$ for $1\leq n\leq 6$ .

The following expression will be used repeatedly:

$$ \psi^{(1)}_{Q^{2},j+1}=-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|},\quad\psi^{(2)}_{Q^{2},j+1}=-\lambda_{j}b_{j}^{(2)}\cdot y_{j}. $$

3rd order: Then we have $\hat{E}_{j}^{(2)}=0$ . Using (3.22) and (4.8), we have

$$ b_{j}^{(3)}=0,\quad m_{j}^{(3)}=0. $$

Then (3.23) and (4.7) yield

$$ \mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(3)}\in\mathcal{H}_{2},\quad\mathrm{Im}\ T_{j}^{(3)}=0. $$

4th order: Then we have

$$ \hat{E}_{j}^{(3)}=-2\psi^{(1)}_{QT_{j+1}^{(3)}}Q-\psi^{(1)}_{Q^{2},j+1}T_{j}^{(3)}-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}T_{j}^{(3)}+i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(3)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot 2\beta. $$

We have $\psi^{(1)}_{QT_{j+1}^{(3)}}=0$ by (4.7) since $QT_{j+1}^{(3)}\in\mathcal{H}_{2}$ . Then by (4.15), we get $\hat{E}_{j}^{(3)}=i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(3)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot 2\beta$ . Therefore,

$$ \mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(3)}=0,\quad\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(3)}\in\mathcal{H}_{2}. $$

Using (3.22) and (4.8), we have

$$ b_{j}^{(4)}=0,\quad m_{j}^{(4)}=0. $$

Then (3.23) and (4.7) yield

$$ \mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(4)}\in\mathcal{H}_{3},\quad\mathrm{Im}\ T_{j}^{(4)}\in\mathcal{H}_{2}. $$

5th order: Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\hat{E}_{j}^{(4)}= \displaystyle-2\psi^{(1)}_{Q\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j+1}^{(4)}}Q-\psi^{(1)}_{Q^{2},j+1}T_{j}^{(4)}-2\psi^{(2)}_{QT_{j+1}^{(3)}}Q-\psi^{(2)}_{Q^{2},j+1}T_{j}^{(3)} \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}b_{j}^{(2)}\cdot y_{j}T_{j}^{(3)}-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}T_{j}^{(4)}+i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(4)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot 2\beta. $$

We have $\psi^{(1)}_{Q\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j+1}^{(4)}}=\psi^{(2)}_{QT_{j+1}^{(3)}}=0$ by (4.7). Then by (4.15), we get $\hat{E}_{j}^{(4)}=i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(4)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot 2\beta$ . Therefore,

$$ \mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(4)}\in\mathcal{H}_{2},\quad\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(4)}\in\mathcal{H}_{3}. $$

Using (3.22) and (4.8), we have

$$ b_{j}^{(5)}=0,\quad m_{j}^{(5)}=0. $$

Then (3.23) and (4.7) yield

$$ \mathrm{Re}\ T_{j}^{(5)}\in\mathcal{H}_{2}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{4},\quad\mathrm{Im}\ T_{j}^{(5)}\in\mathcal{H}_{3}. $$

6th order: Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\hat{E}_{j}^{(5)}= \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}^{-2}\phi_{|T_{j}^{(3)}|^{2}}Q-2\lambda_{j}^{-2}\phi_{QT_{j}^{(3)}}T_{j}^{(3)}-2\psi^{(1)}_{Q\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j+1}^{(5)}}Q-\psi^{(1)}_{Q^{2},j+1}T_{j}^{(5)} \displaystyle-\psi^{(2)}_{Q^{2},j+1}T_{j}^{(4)}-2\psi^{(2)}_{Q\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j+1}^{(4)}}Q-\psi^{(3)}_{Q^{2},j+1}T_{j}^{(3)}-2\psi^{(3)}_{QT_{j+1}^{(3)}}Q \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}b_{j}^{(2)}\cdot y_{j}T_{j}^{(4)}-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}T_{j}^{(5)}+i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(5)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot 2\beta+i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(4)}}{\partial\beta}\big(b_{2}^{(2)}-b_{1}^{(2)}\big). $$

We have $\psi^{(1)}_{Q\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j+1}^{(5)}}=\psi^{(2)}_{Q\mathrm{Re}\ T_{j+1}^{(4)}}=0$ by (4.7). Then by (4.15), we get

$$ \displaystyle\hat{E}_{j}^{(5)}= \displaystyle-\lambda_{j}^{-2}\phi_{|T_{j}^{(3)}|^{2}}Q-2\lambda_{j}^{-2}\phi_{QT_{j}^{(3)}}T_{j}^{(3)}-\psi^{(3)}_{Q^{2},j+1}T_{j}^{(3)}-2\psi^{(3)}_{QT_{j+1}^{(3)}}Q \displaystyle+i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(5)}}{\partial\alpha}\cdot 2\beta+i\frac{\partial T_{j}^{(4)}}{\partial\beta}\big(b_{2}^{(2)}-b_{1}^{(2)}\big). $$

The first line, consisting of terms with $T_{j}^{(3)}$ , is real-valued. Using Property (b) and (4.7), we see these terms are in $\mathcal{H}_{0}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{2}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{4}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{6}$ . Therefore,

$$ \mathrm{Re}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(5)}\in\mathcal{H}_{0}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{2}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{3}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{4}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{6},\quad\mathrm{Im}\ \hat{E}_{j}^{(5)}\in\mathcal{H}_{2}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{3}\oplus\mathcal{H}_{4}. $$

Using (3.22) and (4.8), we have

$$ b_{j}^{(6)}=0,\quad m_{j}^{(6)}=0. $$

We have thus proved Proposition 3.4. ∎

#### Remark 4.1.

With some additional work, one can show that $b_{j}^{(7)}=0$ if and only if $\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}$ . Therefore, in the setting of this paper where we do not make the equal-mass assumption, Proposition 3.4 is optimal.

This also shows that extra cancellation occurs when $\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}$ and one may be able to obtain more precise dynamical information under this assumption, though it is not needed here. In fact, Proposition 4.2 below already gives a longer time scale for the stability of the center dynamics than the time scale we will obtain later in Section 5 for energy estimates.

We now prove the following stability result. Recall our notation that $\alpha=\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1}$ , $\beta=\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}$ and $\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})$ .

#### Proposition 4.2.

Let $C_{e}>0$ and $\lambda_{1}^{0},\lambda_{2}^{0}>0$ . Then there exist $\eta>0$ , $C>0$ and $\bar{r}_{0}>0$ such that for any $r_{0}>\bar{r}_{0}$ and $\frac{1}{2}\eta r_{0}\leq N\leq L\leq\eta r_{0}$ , if $P^{0}(t)$ is an elliptic solution to (1.9) satisfying

$$ r_{0}\leq|\alpha^{0}(t)|\leq C_{e}r_{0},\quad\forall t\geq 0, $$

then the solution $P^{(N)}$ to (4.1) with initial data $P^{(N)}(0)=P^{0}(0)$ satisfies

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &|\alpha^{(N)}(t)-\alpha^{0}(t)|\leq Cr_{0}^{-3/2},\\
&|\beta^{(N)}(t)-\beta^{0}(t)|\leq Cr_{0}^{-3},\\
&|\lambda^{(N)}(t)-\lambda^{0}|\leq Cr_{0}^{-9/2},\end{aligned}\right.\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq r_{0}^{5/2}. $$

#### Remark 4.3.

The time scale $r_{0}^{5/2}$ can be enlarged, at the cost of a weaker upper bound. However, since the time scale in the theorem is $r_{0}^{2}$ , this is sufficient for out purposes.

#### Proof.

By a bootstrap argument, it suffices to prove the following: for any $T_{*}\in[0,r_{0}^{5/2}]$ , if

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &|\alpha^{(N)}(t)-\alpha^{0}(t)|\leq Cr_{0}^{-3/2},\\
&|\beta^{(N)}(t)-\beta^{0}(t)|\leq Cr_{0}^{-3},\\
&|\lambda^{(N)}(t)-\lambda^{0}|\leq Cr_{0}^{-9/2},\end{aligned}\right.\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq T_{*}, $$

then

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} &|\alpha^{(N)}(t)-\alpha^{0}(t)|\leq\frac{1}{2}Cr_{0}^{-3/2},\\
&|\beta^{(N)}(t)-\beta^{0}(t)|\leq\frac{1}{2}Cr_{0}^{-3},\\
&|\lambda^{(N)}(t)-\lambda^{0}|\leq\frac{1}{2}Cr_{0}^{-9/2},\end{aligned}\right.\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq T_{*}. $$

Then (4.36) implies $P^{(N)}$ satisfies (3.51), and thus (3.52) holds since $\frac{1}{2}\eta r_{0}\leq N\leq L\leq\eta r_{0}$ .

The third line is straightforward by integrating the equation for $\lambda$ :

$$ |\lambda^{(N)}(t)-\lambda^{0}|\leq\int_{0}^{t}|M_{1}^{(N)}|+|M_{2}^{(N)}|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-7}t\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-9/2},\quad\forall t\leq T_{*}, $$

so taking $C$ large enough will suffice. It remains to deal with the first two lines.

For an elliptic trajectory of size $r_{0}$ , the relative velocity has size $r_{0}^{-1/2}$ , and the fundamental period has size $r_{0}^{3/2}$ . Thus we normalize the problem by scaling

$$ \tau=r_{0}^{-3/2}t,\quad x^{0}=r_{0}^{-1}\alpha^{0},\quad y^{0}=r_{0}^{1/2}\beta^{0},\quad x=r_{0}^{-1}\alpha^{(N)},\quad y=r_{0}^{1/2}\beta^{(N)}. $$

We have $1\leq|x^{0}|\leq C_{e}$ and $0\leq\tau\leq r_{0}^{-3/2}T_{*}\leq r_{0}$ . Moreover, (1.9) implies

$$ \dot{x}^{0}=2y^{0},\quad\dot{y}^{0}=-m_{0}\frac{x^{0}}{|x^{0}|^{3}}, $$

and (4.1) implies

$$ \dot{x}=2y,\quad\dot{y}=-m_{0}\frac{x}{|x|^{3}}+F, $$

where a dot denotes differentiation with respect to $\tau$ , $m_{0}=\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi}(\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}^{0}}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}^{0}})$ and

$$ \displaystyle F= \displaystyle\ r_{0}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{2}(-1)^{j}\Big(B_{j}^{(N)}(\alpha^{(N)},\beta^{(N)},\lambda^{(N)})-b_{j}^{(2)}(\alpha^{(N)},\beta^{(N)},\lambda^{(N)})\Big) \displaystyle-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi}\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}^{(N)}}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}^{0}}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}^{(N)}}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}^{0}}\Big)\frac{x}{|x|^{3}}. $$

By (4.36) and (3.52), we have

$$ |F|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{2}r_{0}^{-7}+C_{0}r_{0}^{-9/2}\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-9/2}. $$

Let us write $U^{0}=(x^{0},y^{0})$ and $U=(x,y)$ so that (4.40) and (4.41) can be viewed as $6$ -dimensional first-order ODEs of $U^{0}$ and $U$ , respectively. Let $\Phi_{\tau}$ denote the flow associated with (4.40). Namely, for $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ , let $\Phi_{\tau}(Z)$ be the solution of (4.40) with initial data $\Phi_{0}(Z)=Z$ . Strictly speaking, $\Phi_{\tau}$ is only defined on a subset of $\mathbb{R}^{6}$ .

#### Lemma 4.4.

We have the following Duhamel’s formula

$$ U(\tau)-U^{0}(\tau)=\int_{0}^{\tau}D\Phi_{\tau-s}(U(s))(0,F(s))\mathrm{d}s,\quad\forall\tau\geq 0. $$

#### Proof.

Let $W(s)=\Phi_{\tau-s}(U(s))$ and $V(X,Y)=(2Y,-m_{0}\frac{X}{|X|^{3}})$ . Then

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}W(s)=-V(\Phi_{\tau-s}(U(s)))+D\Phi_{\tau-s}(U(s))U^{\prime}(s). $$

From the flow property $\Phi_{s+h}(Z)=\Phi_{s}\Phi_{h}(Z)$ , taking the derivative in $h$ and then setting $h=0$ gives $V(\Phi_{s}(Z))=D\Phi_{s}(Z)V(Z)$ . Then replacing $s$ by $\tau-s$ and $Z$ by $U(s)$ , we obtain

$$ V(\Phi_{\tau-s}(U(s)))=D\Phi_{\tau-s}(U(s))V(U(s)). $$

Note $U^{\prime}(s)=V(U(s))+(0,F(s))$ . We thus deduce

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}W(s)=D\Phi_{\tau-s}(U(s))(0,F(s)). $$

Then (4.45) follows since $W(0)=U^{0}(\tau)$ and $W(\tau)=U(\tau)$ . ∎

Next, we show that $D\Phi_{\tau}$ grows at most linearly in $\tau$ .

#### Lemma 4.5.

Fix $0<\epsilon\ll 1$ . Let $K_{\epsilon}$ be the set of $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ such that $X(\tau)$ describes an ellipse and $\epsilon\leq|X(\tau)|\leq\epsilon^{-1}$ when we write $\Phi_{\tau}(Z)=(X(\tau),Y(\tau))$ . Then

$$ \|D\Phi_{\tau}(Z)\|\lesssim_{\epsilon}1+\tau,\quad\forall Z\in K_{\epsilon},\;\tau\geq 0. $$

#### Proof.

We write $K=K_{\epsilon}$ and let $C$ denote constants depending only on $\epsilon$ .

We first show that $K$ is compact. For $Z=(X_{0},Y_{0})\in K$ , we have $\epsilon\leq|X_{0}|\leq\epsilon^{-1}$ and

$$ |Y_{0}|^{2}-\frac{m_{0}}{|X_{0}|}<0 $$

since $X(\tau)$ describes an ellipse. Thus $|Y_{0}|^{2}\leq 2m_{0}\epsilon^{-1}$ , so $K$ is bounded. Since $X(\tau)$ is continuous in $Z$ and the lower bound of $|X(\tau)|$ ensures that there is no blow-up, we see that $K$ is closed. Therefore, $K$ is a compact set.

For $Z\in K$ , let $a(Z)$ be the semi-major axis of $X(\tau)$ and $T(Z)$ be the fundamental period. By the smooth dependence of parameters and compactness of $K$ , we have

$$ |DT(Z)|\leq C,\quad\forall Z\in K. $$

Moreover, $T(Z)/a(Z)^{3}$ is constant by Kepler’s third law. Since $\epsilon\leq|X(\tau)|\leq\epsilon^{-1}$ , we have $C^{-1}\leq a(Z)\leq C$ and thus $C^{-1}\leq T(Z)\leq C,\;\forall Z\in K$ . Then by the smoothness of $\Phi_{\tau}(Z)$ in both $\tau$ and $Z$ , we have

$$ \|D\Phi_{\tau}(Z)\|\leq C,\quad\forall Z\in K,\;\tau\in[0,T(Z)]. $$

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ . For any $\tau\geq 0$ , let $s(Z)=\tau-nT(Z)$ . Then

$$ \Phi_{\tau}(Z)=\Phi_{s(Z)}(Z). $$

We differentiate both sides in $Z$ . Since $Ds(Z)=-nDT(Z)$ , we get

$$ D\Phi_{\tau}(Z)=D\Phi_{s(Z)}(Z)-nV(\Phi_{s(Z)}(Z))DT(Z). $$

Therefore, if $s(Z)\in[0,T(Z)]$ , or equivalently, $\tau\in[nT(Z),(n+1)T(Z)]$ , then

$$ \|D\Phi_{\tau}(Z)\|\leq C+Cn. $$

This implies the desired estimate since $n\leq\tau/T(Z)$ and $T(Z)\geq C^{-1}$ . ∎

The estimate now follows from a straightforward calculation. By (4.36), if $r_{0}$ is large enough, then $U(s)$ remains close to $U^{0}(s)$ , and thus $U(s)\in K_{\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon$ depending on $C_{e}$ . We can then apply Lemma 4.5 to get

$$ \|D\Phi_{\tau-s}(U(s))\|\leq C_{0}(1+\tau). $$

Note that $0\leq t\leq T_{*}$ implies $0\leq\tau\leq r_{0}$ . Using (4.45) and (4.44), we obtain

$$ |U(\tau)-U^{0}(\tau)|\leq C_{0}\tau(1+\tau)r_{0}^{-9/2}\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-5/2},\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq T_{*}. $$

Finally, we scale back to the original parameters and we get

$$ |\alpha^{(N)}(t)-\alpha^{0}(t)|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-3/2},\quad|\beta^{(N)}(t)-\beta^{0}(t)|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-3},\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq T_{*}. $$

Then the desired estimate follows by taking $C$ large enough. ∎

## 5. Modulation and error estimates

In this section, we prove the main theorem. We first reduce Theorem 1 to a statement about the approximate solution.

#### Proposition 5.1.

Given $K>1$ and $\delta>0$ , there exist $\nu>0$ , $\eta>0$ , $\bar{r}_{0}>0$ such that for any $r_{0}>\bar{r}_{0}$ , there exists $\kappa>0$ with the following property.

If $\frac{1}{2}\eta r_{0}\leq N\leq L\leq\eta r_{0}$ and $P^{(N)}(t)$ is a solution to (4.1) with

$$ |\alpha^{(N)}(t)|\geq r_{0},\quad|\beta^{(N)}(t)|\leq K,\quad K^{-1}\leq\lambda_{j}^{(N)}(t)\leq K,\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq\nu r_{0}^{2} $$

and $\gamma_{1}^{(N)}(t)$ , $\gamma_{2}^{(N)}(t)$ satisfy

$$ \dot{\gamma}_{j}^{(N)}=\frac{1}{(\lambda_{j}^{(N)})^{2}}-|\beta_{j}^{(N)}|^{2}-\dot{\beta}_{j}^{(N)}\cdot\alpha_{j}^{(N)}+\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}^{(N)}}\frac{1}{|\alpha^{(N)}|},\quad j=1,2, $$

then for $u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ ,

$$ \Big\|u_{0}-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(0,\cdot)\Big\|_{H^{1}}<\kappa $$

implies

$$ \Big\|u(t,\cdot)-(g_{1}^{(N)}Q)(t,\cdot)-(g_{2}^{(N)}Q)(t,\cdot)\Big\|_{H^{1}}<\delta,\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq\nu r_{0}^{2}, $$

where $u$ is the solution to (1.1) with $u(0)=u_{0}$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 1 assuming Proposition 5.1.

For an elliptic solution $P^{0}$ to (1.9) as in Theorem 1, take $N$ , $L$ such that $\frac{1}{2}\eta r_{0}\leq N\leq L\leq\eta r_{0}$ and let $P^{(N)}$ be the solution to (4.1) with the same initial data. Let $\gamma_{j}^{(N)}$ also have the same initial data as $\gamma_{j}$ .

We take $R_{0}=R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(0,\cdot)$ , which satisfies (1.14) because of (3.53). Proposition 4.2 implies (5.1) for $K$ and $r_{0}$ large enough, so we may apply Proposition 5.1 to get (5.4).

Finally, we deduce (1.15) from (5.4) by using Proposition 4.2 and a similar estimate regarding the phase $\gamma_{j}^{(N)}$ for $r_{0}$ large enough. ∎

Now it remains to prove Proposition 5.1. The strategy is similar to the proof of [9, Proposition 3.3] or [19, Proposition 3.2], especially Step 1–3 below, except for the Grönwall argument. The main difference is that since we are studying the elliptic case, we do not gain any decay by taking $t$ large enough, as opposed to [9, 19]. Instead, the final estimate relies essentially on the uniform smallness of the approximation error obtained in Proposition 3.9. The choice $N\sim r_{0}$ ensures that the constants $c_{0},C_{0}$ there do not depend on $N$ .

#### Proof of Proposition 5.1.

In the proof, we will let $c_{0},C_{0}$ denote positive constants that depend only on $K$ . We write $f=O_{0}(|g|)$ if $|f|\leq C_{0}|g|$ .

Step 1: Let $u$ be the solution to (1.1) with $u(0,\cdot)=u_{0}$ satisfying (5.3). Using a bootstrap argument and the inverse function theorem, it is standard that for $r_{0}$ large enough and $\kappa$ small enough, there exists $g(t)$ such that if

$$ \varepsilon(t,x)=u(t,x)-R_{g}^{(N)}(t,x), $$

then $\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}$ is small, and for $t\in[0,\nu r_{0}^{2}]$ and $j=1,2$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\Big)=\mathrm{Re}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(y_{j}V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(\Lambda V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big)=\mathrm{Im}\Big(\varepsilon(t),g_{j}\big(\nabla V_{j}^{(N)}\big)\Big)=0. $$

In particular, we have

$$ \|g(0)-g^{(N)}(0)\|<C_{0}\kappa,\quad\|\varepsilon(0)\|_{H^{1}}<C_{0}\kappa. $$

A detailed proof of this statement can be found in [19, Lemma 3.3].

To simplify notation, we write $R_{j}=R_{j,g}^{(N)}$ , $R=R_{g}^{(N)}$ , $M_{j}=M_{j}^{(N)}$ , $B_{j}=B_{j}^{(N)}$ , $V_{j}=V_{j}^{(N)}$ , $S_{j}=S_{j}^{(N)}$ and $\Psi=\Psi^{(N)}$ . We have

$$ i\partial_{t}\varepsilon+\Delta\varepsilon-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}R-\phi_{|R|^{2}}\varepsilon=\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)-\Psi-\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}S_{j}(t,x)e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}, $$

where

$$ \mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)=2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\varepsilon+\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}R+\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}\varepsilon. $$

Step 2: We estimate the closeness between $g$ and $g^{(N)}$ in terms of $\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}$ .

Define the modulation error

$$ \displaystyle Mod(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{2}\Bigg( \displaystyle\Big|\dot{\alpha}_{j}(t)-2\beta_{j}(t)\Big|+\Big|\dot{\beta}_{j}(t)-B_{j}(P(t))\Big|+\Big|\dot{\lambda}_{j}(t)-M_{j}(P(t))\Big| \displaystyle+\bigg|\dot{\gamma}_{j}(t)-\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}(t)}+|\beta_{j}(t)|^{2}+\dot{\beta}_{j}(t)\cdot\alpha_{j}(t)-\frac{\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{4\pi\lambda_{j+1}}\frac{1}{|\alpha|}\bigg|\Bigg). $$

Let $\theta_{j}=g_{j}\theta$ , where $\theta(t,x)$ satisfies

$$ |\theta(t,x)|\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}|x|},\quad\forall t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

By (5.8), we can compute

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{Im}\int\varepsilon\overline{\theta_{j}}= \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\int\varepsilon\left(\overline{i\partial_{t}\theta_{j}+\Delta\theta_{j}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R})}R-\phi_{|R|^{2}}\theta_{j}}\right) \displaystyle+\mathrm{Re}\int\Big(\Psi-\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)\Big)\overline{\theta_{j}}+\sum_{k=1}^{2}\mathrm{Re}\int\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}^{2}}S_{k}(t,x)e^{i\gamma_{k}+i\beta_{k}\cdot x}\overline{\theta_{k}}. $$

By (3.52) and (5.11), we have

$$ i\partial_{t}\theta_{j}+\Delta\theta_{j}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\left(i\lambda_{j}^{2}\partial_{t}\theta+\Delta\theta-\theta\right)e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+O_{0}\left(\left(r_{0}^{-1}+Mod\right)e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right). $$

By the localization of $V_{j}$ , (5.11) and the proof of Proposition 3.9, we have

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R})}R \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta\overline{V_{j}})}V_{j}e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+O_{0}\left(\big(r_{0}^{-1}+e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\big)e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right) $$

and

$$ \phi_{|R|^{2}}\theta_{j}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\phi_{|V_{j}|^{2}}\theta e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+O_{0}\left(\big(r_{0}^{-1}+e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\big)e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right). $$

Collecting the terms of degree $1$ in $\theta$ , we define

$$ L_{j}\theta:=-\Delta\theta+\theta+2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta\overline{V_{j}})}V_{j}+\phi_{|V_{j}|^{2}}\theta. $$

This is the linearized operator around the profile $V_{j}$ , and we have

$$ \displaystyle i\partial_{t}\theta_{j}+\Delta\theta_{j}-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\theta_{j}\overline{R})}R-\phi_{|R|^{2}}\theta_{j} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\left(i\lambda_{j}^{2}\partial_{t}\theta-L_{j}\theta\right)e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+O_{0}\Big(\big(r_{0}^{-1}+Mod\big)\max_{k}e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{k}|}\Big). $$

Thus, from (5.12), (3.55) and (5.11), we get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathrm{Im}\int\varepsilon\overline{\theta_{j}}= \displaystyle\mathrm{Re}\int\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\overline{\left(i\lambda_{j}^{2}\partial_{t}\theta-L_{j}\theta\right)e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}}+\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{6}}\mathrm{Re}\int S_{j}\overline{\theta} \displaystyle+O_{0}\left(\Big(r_{0}^{-1}+Mod\Big)\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\right). $$

We will take $\theta$ to be $iV_{j}$ , $\nabla V_{j}$ , $\Lambda V_{j}$ and $iy_{j}V_{j}$ , which correspond to $\gamma_{j}$ , $\alpha_{j}$ , $\lambda_{j}$ and $\beta_{j}$ , respectively. By (5.6), the left-hand side always vanishes. By (3.53) and (3.52), we always have

$$ \partial_{t}\theta=O_{0}\left(\left(r_{0}^{-1}+Mod\right)e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right). $$

By (3.53) and (1.6), we know

$$ W_{j}:=-\Delta V_{j}+V_{j}+\phi_{|V_{j}|^{2}}V_{j} $$

satisfies $|W_{j}|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-1}e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}$ . Direct computation yields

$$ \begin{gathered}L_{j}(iV_{j})=iW_{j},\quad L_{j}(\Lambda V_{j})=(\Lambda+2)W_{j}-2V_{j},\\
L_{j}(\nabla V_{j})=\nabla W_{j},\quad L_{j}(iy_{j}V_{j})=iy_{j}W_{j}-2i\nabla V_{j}.\end{gathered} $$

By (5.6), we always have

$$ L_{j}\theta=f+O_{0}\left(r_{0}^{-1}e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right), $$

where $f$ is a function such that $\mathrm{Re}\int\varepsilon(\overline{g_{j}f})=0$ . Thus

$$ \mathrm{Re}\int\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda_{j}^{4}}\overline{L_{j}\theta\ e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}}=O_{0}\left(r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}\right). $$

Finally, using (3.17) and (3.53) and summing over the four choices of $\theta$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\theta}\sum_{j=1}^{2}\left|\mathrm{Re}\int S_{j}\overline{\theta}\right|\geq c_{0}Mod-C_{0}r_{0}^{-1}Mod. $$

Therefore, combining (5.19), (5.23), (5.24) and taking $r_{0}$ large enough, we obtain

$$ Mod(t)\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}+C_{0}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}. $$

Step 3: We give an upper bound for $\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}$ .

Let $\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}$ be smooth cutoff functions such that

$$ \begin{gathered}\varphi_{j}(t,x)\geq 0,\quad\sum_{j=1}^{2}\varphi_{j}(t,x)\equiv 1,\quad|\partial_{t}\varphi_{j}|+|\nabla\varphi_{j}|\leq C_{0}r^{-1},\\
\varphi_{j}(t,x)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &1,\quad|x-\alpha_{j}(t)|\leq c_{0}r(t),\\
&0,\quad|x-\alpha_{j+1}(t)|\leq c_{0}r(t).\end{aligned}\right.\end{gathered} $$

By (3.53), we have

$$ |\varphi_{j}R-R_{j}|\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r(t)},\quad\forall t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

Define $\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon)=\mathcal{G}_{1}+\mathcal{G}_{2}+\mathcal{G}_{3}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{1}=\int|\nabla\varepsilon|^{2}+\int\phi_{|R|^{2}}|\varepsilon|^{2}-2\int|\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}|^{2}+2\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}|\varepsilon|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int|\nabla\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}|^{2}, \displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{2}\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\varphi_{j}|\varepsilon|^{2},\qquad\mathcal{G}_{3}=-2\sum_{j=1}^{2}\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(\nabla\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon}). $$

By [19, Proposition 4.1], for $r_{0}$ large enough, we have $\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon)\geq c_{0}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}$ .

Then we compute

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}= \displaystyle-2\mathrm{Im}\int i\partial_{t}\overline{\varepsilon}\left(\Delta\varepsilon-\phi_{|R|^{2}}\varepsilon-2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}R-\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon)\right) \displaystyle+4\mathrm{Re}\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\varepsilon\partial_{t}\overline{R}+2\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\partial_{t}R\overline{R})}|\varepsilon|^{2}+2\mathrm{Re}\int\phi_{|\varepsilon|^{2}}\varepsilon\partial_{t}\overline{R}. $$

By (5.8) and (3.55), the first line is $O_{0}\left(\big(e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}+Mod\big)\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}\right)$ .

For the second line, using (3.52), we have

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}R_{j} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}\left(-\dot{\alpha}_{j}\cdot\nabla V_{j}-i(\dot{\gamma}_{j}-\dot{\beta}_{j}\cdot\alpha_{j})V_{j}\right)e^{i\gamma_{j}+i\beta_{j}\cdot x}+O_{0}\left(r_{0}^{-1}e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right) \displaystyle=-2\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla R_{j}+i\big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\big)R_{j}+O_{0}\left(\left(r_{0}^{-1}+Mod\right)e^{-c_{0}|x-\alpha_{j}|}\right). $$

Combining this with (5.25), we get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}t}= \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{2}\Bigg(4\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Im}(\varepsilon\overline{R_{j}})-8\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla\overline{R_{j}}) \displaystyle-4\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla R_{j}\overline{R_{j}})}|\varepsilon|^{2}\Bigg) \displaystyle+O_{0}\left(e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\right). $$

Using (5.26), we have

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{2}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\sum_{j=1}^{2}2\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(i\partial_{t}\varepsilon\overline{\varepsilon})+O_{0}\left(r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\right). $$

Then by (5.8) and (3.55), we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{2}}{\mathrm{d}t} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{2}2\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Im}(2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}R\overline{\varepsilon}) \displaystyle+O_{0}\left(e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+Mod\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\right). $$

Finally, using (5.25) and (5.27), we get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{2}}{\mathrm{d}t} \displaystyle=-\sum_{j=1}^{2}4\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda_{j}^{2}}+|\beta_{j}|^{2}\Big)\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Im}(\varepsilon\overline{R_{j}}) \displaystyle+O_{0}\left(e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\right). $$

Similarly, we can compute

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}_{3}}{\mathrm{d}t} \displaystyle=-\sum_{j=1}^{2}4\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Re}(i\partial_{t}\varepsilon\nabla\overline{\varepsilon})+O_{0}\left(r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\right) \displaystyle=-\sum_{j=1}^{2}4\beta_{j}\int\varphi_{j}\mathrm{Re}\left(2\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}R\nabla\overline{\varepsilon}+\phi_{|R|^{2}}\varepsilon\nabla\overline{\varepsilon}\right) \displaystyle+O_{0}\left(e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+Mod\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{2}\left(8\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\overline{R})}\mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla\overline{R_{j}})+4\int\phi_{\mathrm{Re}(\beta_{j}\cdot\nabla R_{j}\overline{R_{j}})}|\varepsilon|^{2}\right) \displaystyle+O_{0}\left(e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}\right). $$

Combining (5.30), (5.33), (5.34), we deduce

$$ \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon(t))\right|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-1}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}+C_{0}\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}^{3}. $$

By the coercivity of $\mathcal{G}$ , we have

$$ \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{G}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-1}\mathcal{G}+C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\mathcal{G}^{\frac{1}{2}}+C_{0}\mathcal{G}^{\frac{3}{2}}. $$

Then using Grönwall’s inequality, we deduce

$$ \mathcal{G}(t)\leq C_{0}\sup_{\tau\in[0,t]}\left(e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}\mathcal{G}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\tau)+C_{0}\mathcal{G}^{\frac{3}{2}}(\tau)\right)e^{\frac{C_{0}t}{r_{0}}}+C_{0}\kappa^{2}e^{\frac{C_{0}t}{r_{0}}}. $$

Since $t\leq\nu r_{0}^{2}$ , by taking $\nu$ small enough, then $r_{0}$ large enough, and finally $\kappa$ small enough, we obtain $\mathcal{G}(\varepsilon(t))\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}$ by bootstrap. Using the coercivity of $\mathcal{G}$ , this yields

$$ \|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}. $$

Step 4: We give an upper bound for $|g-g^{(N)}|$ independent of $\|\varepsilon\|_{H^{1}}$ .

Now (5.25) implies $Mod(t)\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}$ . Recall $\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})$ . Let

$$ F(t)=r_{0}^{-2}\big|\alpha(t)-\alpha^{(N)}(t)\big|^{2}+\big|\beta(t)-\beta^{(N)}(t)\big|^{2}+\big|\lambda(t)-\lambda^{(N)}(t)\big|^{2}. $$

Then

$$ \dot{F}\leq C_{0}F^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big(r_{0}^{-1}\big|\dot{\alpha}-\dot{\alpha}^{(N)}\big|+\big|\dot{\beta}-\dot{\beta}^{(N)}\big|+\big|\dot{\lambda}-\dot{\lambda}^{(N)}\big|\Big). $$

Since $P^{(N)}$ satisfies (4.1) and by the definition of $Mod$ , we get

$$ \dot{F}\leq C_{0}F^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigg(Mod+r_{0}^{-1}\big|\beta-\beta^{(N)}\big|+\sum_{j=1}^{2}\Big[\big|B_{j}(P)-B_{j}(P^{(N)})\big|+\big|M_{j}(P)-M_{j}(P^{(N)})\big|\Big]\bigg). $$

Using (3.52) and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have

$$ \big|B_{j}(P)-B_{j}(P^{(N)})\big|+\big|M_{j}(P)-M_{j}(P^{(N)})\big|\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-1}F^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

We thus obtain

$$ \dot{F}\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-1}F+C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}F^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Then we deduce $F(t)\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}$ for $t\leq\nu r_{0}^{2}$ by Grönwall’s inequality as above. This gives the upper bound for $|P-P^{(N)}|$ . The estimate for $\gamma$ follows by direct integration.

In conclusion, in Step 3, we obtain

$$ \|u(t,\cdot)-R_{g}^{(N)}(t,\cdot)\|_{H^{1}}\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}},\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq\nu r_{0}^{2} $$

and in Step 4, we obtain

$$ |g-g^{(N)}|\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}},\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq\nu r_{0}^{2}. $$

Thus we deduce

$$ \|u(t,\cdot)-R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(t,\cdot)\|_{H^{1}}\leq C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}},\quad\forall 0\leq t\leq\nu r_{0}^{2}. $$

By (3.53), we have

$$ \|R_{g^{(N)}}^{(N)}(t,\cdot)-(g_{1}^{(N)}Q)(t,\cdot)-(g_{2}^{(N)}Q)(t,\cdot)\|_{H^{1}}\leq C_{0}r_{0}^{-3}. $$

Therefore, we conclude (5.4) by taking $r_{0}$ large enough so that $C_{0}e^{-c_{0}r_{0}}+C_{0}r_{0}^{-3}<\delta$ . ∎
